question: A 45-year-old man with 15 years of type 2 diabetes is found on fundoscopy to have microaneurysms, dot-blot haemorrhages, hard exudates, cotton wool spots, and venous beading in all four quadrants. There are NO new vessels visible anywhere. What is the MOST appropriate classification?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Mild NPDR is characterised only by microaneurysms. The presence of cotton wool spots and venous beading places this in a more advanced category.
Incorrect. PDR requires the presence of new vessels (neovascularisation) — either at the disc (NVD) or elsewhere (NVE). The question explicitly states no new vessels are present.

Correct. Severe NPDR is defined by the 4-2-1 rule: haemorrhages in all 4 quadrants, venous beading in ≥2 quadrants, OR intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMA) in ≥1 quadrant. Cotton wool spots indicate ischaemia but no new vessels = still NPDR.

answers.text: Diabetic macular oedema — a separate classification requiring immediate anti-VEGF

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Diabetic macular oedema is an additional finding that can coexist with any stage of retinopathy but is a separate classification. The question asks about the retinopathy stage, not the macular status.

overallFeedback.feedback: Critical rule: the only feature that converts NPDR to PDR is neovascularisation (new vessels at disc or elsewhere). All other changes — even severe ischaemia — remain NPDR. Learn the 4-2-1 rule.
Excellent. The 4-2-1 rule defines severe NPDR. Remember: NO new vessels = NPDR; ANY new vessels = PDR. This distinction determines referral urgency and laser threshold.
